The way this collector is contacting you may itself be illegal under the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act: calling before 8am or after 9pm, calling you at work after being told to stop, telling another person (like your sister) about the debt, or calling many times a day can each violate the law (15 U.S.C. § 1692c/§ 1692d). Keep your call log. Can you note the dates, times, and who they contacted? [Authority: 15 U.S.C. § 1692c(a) (calls before 8am/after 9pm, at work after notice); § 1692b/§ 1692c(b) (third-party disclosure of the debt); § 1692d (harassing volume)]

The collector said they will garnish your wages or freeze your bank account 'by the end of the month.' In Minnesota a collector generally CANNOT garnish or freeze anything without first suing you and getting a court judgment (Minn. Stat. § 571.71) — and you said no court papers were ever served. Threatening action they cannot legally take is itself an FDCPA violation (15 U.S.C. § 1692e). Have you ever been served with any lawsuit or court papers about this debt? [Authority: 15 U.S.C. § 1692e(4)–(5) (threat of action that cannot legally be taken); Minn. Stat. § 571.71 (garnishment generally requires a judgment first)]

You said your income is Social Security disability plus a little part-time pay. Social Security and SSDI are protected by law from most debt collection (42 U.S.C. § 407), and Minnesota gives extra protection to low wages and exempt funds in a bank account (Minn. Stat. § 571.912/§ 571.922). You may be effectively 'judgment-proof.' Is Social Security your only regular income, and is it direct-deposited? [Authority: 42 U.S.C. § 407(a) (Social Security/SSDI exempt from garnishment); Minn. Stat. § 571.912/§ 571.922 (exemption-notice process; wage-exemption floor)]

questions.question_text: Do you remember if any debt collectors ever called you outside of 8am to 9pm?
questions.rationale: Understanding if the calls occurred at inconvenient times can help identify violations of your rights.

questions.question_text: Have you ever informed the debt collector not to call you at your workplace? Did they continue to call there afterwards?
questions.rationale: This helps determine if your privacy rights were infringed upon regarding workplace calls.

questions.question_text: Have you noticed if the debt collector has shared information about your debt with anyone else, like friends or family?
questions.rationale: This will help assess whether your privacy rights were violated by third-party disclosures.

questions.question_text: Have you experienced any financial losses or difficulties as a result of the debt collection actions?
questions.rationale: Gathering information about damages will help understand the impact and may support potential claims for relief.

questions.question_text: Have you received any notices about wage garnishment? If so, what was the timeframe given in that notice?
questions.rationale: Understanding the timeframe can help evaluate whether timely responses were made to protect against garnishment.

questions.question_text: What kind of income do you currently have, and is it just Social Security disability, or do you have other sources?
questions.rationale: This helps in assessing whether you might qualify for income exemptions under the law.

questions.question_text: Have you been served with any court papers or lawsuit notices regarding this debt?

questions.rationale: Understanding your response timeline can reveal any potential missteps in protecting your rights.

deadlines.event_text: I haven't paid on that card since August 2020.
deadlines.citation: Minn. Stat. § 541.05, subd. 1(1) (6-year limitations period on a contract/credit-card debt); Minn. Stat. § 541.053 (a payment or written acknowledgment can restart the clock — but cannot revive a debt already time-barred).
deadlines.hedge: In Minnesota a credit-card/contract debt generally becomes time-barred about 6 years after your last payment or default — after that, the collector can ask but cannot force you to pay. WARNING: making even a small payment (or admitting the debt in writing) BEFORE that date can RESTART the whole 6-year clock. Do NOT pay or promise anything until a lawyer confirms the exact limitations date. Estimated — confirm the exact date with the court or a lawyer.

deadlines.event_text: The letter came in the mail June 25, its dated June 20, and it says I owe $2,483.17.
deadlines.citation: 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a)–(b) (FDCPA debt-validation period: 30 days from RECEIPT of the collector's initial written notice; a timely written dispute forces collection to cease until the debt is verified).
deadlines.hedge: Under the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act you generally have 30 days from when you RECEIVED the collector's first letter to dispute or demand verification of the debt in writing (this window runs from the date you received the letter, not the date printed on it). A written dispute mailed in time forces the collector to stop until they verify the debt. Estimated — confirm the exact date with the court or a lawyer.
